title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
A fake American think tank, funded by the Israeli government and routed through a European advertising firm, published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days. The reports presented one-sided positions on contentious topics including Israeli military actions and Gaza's humanitarian situation, framed as neutral academic research with citations from respected organizations. The operation exploited a failure mode in AI chatbot deployment: systems trained to cite authoritative-seeming sources without verification of those sources' legitimacy or independence.

The fake think tank used specialized platforms designed to optimize content for AI systems, ensuring chatbots would treat the reports as credible material and cite them in responses. This represents deployment of AI without adequate safeguards against poisoned training data or adversarial input designed specifically to manipulate model outputs. The reports included caveats that undermined criticism of Israeli actions, showing intentional framing rather than neutral research.

It is not established what measures, if any, the AI companies whose systems were targeted took to verify sources or detect the campaign. Israeli officials later expressed frustration that the operation did not improve Israel's standing in American public opinion, but the actual impact on chatbot outputs and user beliefs remains unreported.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days to manipulate artificial intelligence chatbots into promoting pro-Israel arguments. The website, which does not exist as a legal entity, presented one-sided positions on contentious topics including Israeli war crimes and Gaza's humanitarian situation, framed as neutral academic research. The reports were designed to appear authoritative with citations from respected organizations, though they repeatedly included caveats that undermined criticism of Israel's actions.

The operation was part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government and routed through European advertising firm Havas Media. Companies like Piro Inc used specialized platforms designed to optimize content for AI systems, ensuring chatbots would cite these sources in their responses. Israeli officials later expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy effort failed to improve Israel's declining standing in American public opinion, with polling showing Americans increasingly sympathetic to Palestinians and critical of Israeli military actions in Gaza.
